title: Greedy Best-First: Fast Streets, Smart Turns ⚡
description: Watch how Greedy Best-First finds a route across real street-like nodes by always expanding the most promising frontier first. In this visualization on Copenhagen (Vesterbro), you’ll see how heuristic guidance can race toward the goal—sometimes at the cost of optimality.
ig_caption:
🚦 Greedy Best-First is sprinting through Copenhagen (Vesterbro)! 🗺️✨

Here’s the idea in graph-search terms: we model a street map as a weighted (or unweighted) graph where intersections are nodes and road segments are edges. Greedy Best-First prioritizes a frontier node by **f(n) = h(n)** only—meaning it chooses the next step that *appears* closest to the target using a heuristic like straight-line distance to the goal. 🎯

That heuristic pull makes it feel incredibly fast because it aggressively commits toward the goal, but since it ignores the true path cost so far (**no g(n)** like A*), it can take longer routes or get “lured” by an optimistic shortcut. 📉⚠️

In this reel, each frame shows the priority queue selecting the next best-looking intersection until the path to the destination is reconstructed. 🧠💡

👉 Want a follow-up showing A* vs Greedy Best-First on the *same* map? Drop a comment with “A*” and hit like!
fb_caption:
🚗💡 Greedy Best-First on a real street-node graph in Copenhagen (Vesterbro)!

In this visualization, we treat intersections as nodes and roads as edges, then run a graph search that always expands the node that looks closest to the destination using a heuristic (f(n)=h(n)). Because it follows the goal estimate without accounting for distance traveled so far, it’s often quick—but not guaranteed to be optimal.

Greedy Best-First Pathfinding Visualization on Real Street-Map Style Graphs (Copenhagen Vesterbro) ⚡

In this YouTube Shorts reel, we animate Greedy Best-First search: intersections = nodes, roads = edges, and the algorithm uses f(n)=h(n) to expand the most promising frontier toward the goal. You’ll see heuristic-driven priority queue behavior, fast greedy routing, and why it may trade optimality for speed.
